text: Organizations often adopt safety management system or behavior-based system approaches to managing their safety functions in an attempt to achieve performance excellence. Organizations typically prefer adopting one system versus the other probably due to both pragmatic (e.g., resource and implementation constraints) and philosophical reasons. Commonly adopted safety management system approaches are described in consensus standards such as OHSAS 18001:2007 (British Standards Institute, 2007), ANSI/AIHA Z10-2012 (American National Standards Institute, 2012), and the OSHA's Voluntary Protection Program (VPP) (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2011). Second, safety management systems tend to be institutionalized through policies, plans, procedures, and processes and therefore are not easily and readily adaptable to the natural and inevitable variations occurring in work being conducted and the hazards being encountered. Lastly, humans, who are fallible, design and implement safety management systems. Therefore, the lifeblood of a safety management system is shared with the managers and workers who have birthed the system and have given it daily life (and sometimes death). From a behavioral perspective, workers bring their beliefs, values, and vision to the design and implementation of safety management systems and ultimately in performing work. Second, human behavior is inherently variable and unpredictable, making it difficult to anticipate every possible action or decision that might lead to an error or an accident. No safety management system, regardless of its sophistication, can entirely eliminate the risk of human error. This unpredictability highlights the importance of fostering a safety culture that encourages mindfulness, adaptability, and continuous learning among employees at all levels. Moreover, communication plays a crucial role in bridging the gap between safety management systems and behavioral approaches. Effective communication ensures that safety policies are not only understood but are also internalized by the workforce. Second, even if the most effective safety management system were implemented perfectly, there is no guarantee that it would prevent every accident. Third, no matter how good the safety management system is, there is always the possibility that humans will make mistakes. Fourth, people and machines are imperfect. Fifth, any complex system has many interdependent parts, and small errors in one part may cause large errors elsewhere in the system. Sixth, safety management systems require humans to implement them, and humans are fallible. Finally, the safety management system itself can be a source of error and failure. This recognition of the limitations of safety management systems and the inevitability of human error highlights the need for a more comprehensive approach to safety management. The human performance approach, which acknowledges the role of organizational factors in shaping human behavior and decision-making, offers a promising framework for understanding and mitigating the causes of human error. One of the key advantages of the human performance approach is its focus on understanding the underlying causes of human error, rather than simply addressing the symptoms. By identifying and addressing the latent organizational weaknesses that give rise to error precursors, organizations can create a safer and more resilient work environment.
